title: Order in the Temple
sum: Clement turns from the order of creation and of the body to the order God gave Israel's worship. God fixed the times of the offerings, the place, and the people who bring them. The high priest, the priests, the Levites and the layperson each have their own part, and those who keep to it are "acceptable and blessed."

The chapter prepares the argument of 41-44. If God cared so much about order in Israel's worship, he cares about it in the church too. It also holds the Greek word behind "layperson" (see the note at 40:5).

views.H: Clement describes the Temple service in the present tense (see 41:2) and reasons from it as from a fixed pattern of order, not as rules Christians themselves keep.
views.J: The four ranks follow the law closely: the high priest's own duties (Leviticus 16), the priests at the altar (Numbers 18:1-7), the Levites' service (Numbers 3:5-10), and the ordinary Israelite. Clement treats the law of Moses as a true picture of what God wants.
views.O: Clement sets Israel's priests and Levites beside the church's leaders, but he states only the principle of order; he does not call Christian ministers priests (see the note at 40:5 and the cards at Hebrews 7:23-28 and 1 Peter 2:5-9).

echoes: Leviticus 16; Numbers 3:5-10; Numbers 18:1-7; Deuteronomy 12:5-14; 1 Corinthians 14:40; Hebrews 8:3-5; 1 Peter 2:5-9

settings.by: The church of God at Rome, writing as one body ("we"); tradition names Clement as the writer
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, addressed as "brothers" and "beloved"
settings.when: Toward the end of the first century (Lake: between 75 and 110, most likely the 90s), after the Corinthians removed some of their elders
settings.why: To show from the law the Corinthians knew that God fixes who serves and how, so that removing proper leaders is breaking God's order.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Each in his own rank
sum: Clement draws the lesson: "each of us must please God in his own rank." Sacrifices were offered only in Jerusalem, only before the sanctuary, only after the high priest had checked the animal. Those who broke the law's order faced death. "The more knowledge we have been counted worthy of, the more danger we stand in."
The verbs about the Temple are in the present tense. Some have used this to date the letter before the Temple fell in AD 70; Lightfoot and Lake did not (see the note at 41:2).

views.H: The present tense of 41:2 is the main argument for a date before AD 70. Lightfoot answers that Josephus and the Epistle of Barnabas also describe the Temple in the present long after its fall; Lake dates the letter from chapters 5, 42 and 44 to 75-110.
views.N: The argument from the lesser to the greater (41:4) echoes the method of Hebrews 2:2-3 and 10:28-29, and of Luke 12:48.
views.J: Clement knows the kinds of sacrifice (the daily offering, vows, sin and guilt offerings) and the rule of one place (Deuteronomy 12), and he adds the inspection of the animal by the high priest and the ministers, which the law implies but does not describe.
views.G: Tagma, "rank," is a word of the army, as in 37:3, where each soldier "in his own rank, carries out what the emperor and the commanders order."

deep.b: Clement says the sacrifices "are presented" in Jerusalem. If he meant that literally, the letter was written before AD 70. Lightfoot reports that such an early date "has been thought," and replies that "to this very early date however there are insuperable objections": chapter 44 speaks of elders appointed by the apostles' successors, and chapter 5 looks back on the deaths of Peter and Paul. He reads the present tense as referring to the lasting record in the law, as Josephus does in his Antiquities (about AD 93) and the Epistle of Barnabas in its chapter 7. Lake does not use the verse at all for his date of 75-110.

echoes: Deuteronomy 12:5-14; Leviticus 22:17-25; Numbers 18:7; Luke 12:48; Hebrews 2:2-3; Hebrews 10:28-29

title: From God, through Christ, to the apostles
sum: Here is the center of the letter's case. Christ was sent from God, the apostles from Christ. Sure of the resurrection and full of the Spirit, they preached in country and city and appointed their "firstfruits," tested by the Spirit, as overseers and deacons for future believers. This was "nothing new," Clement says, and he quotes "Scripture" for it: "I will appoint their overseers in righteousness and their deacons in faith" (42:5), a reshaped form of Isaiah 60:17 in the Greek.

Two questions run through every later reading of this chapter: whether Clement's "overseers" are the same men as the "elders" of 44:5, and how his quotation relates to the Isaiah of the Hebrew and the Greek Bible.

views.H: The chapter is a historical claim about how the first churches were organized, written a generation or two after the apostles. Historians weigh it beside Acts and the Pastoral Letters; Lightfoot read it as showing two offices, overseers (also called elders) and deacons.
views.N: The pair "overseers and deacons" is that of Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:1-13; the testing is that of 1 Timothy 3:10; the sending chain echoes John 20:21. Clement adds the claim that the apostles planned for those who would come later.
views.J: The "Scripture" is Isaiah 60:17 in the Greek, reshaped: the Hebrew has peace and righteousness as Zion's governors; the Greek, "rulers in peace and overseers in righteousness"; Clement, "overseers in righteousness and deacons in faith."
views.O: The Catholic Catechism cites chapters 42 and 44 for the apostles' provision for successors (CCC 861) and 42:4 and 44:3 for the apostles choosing collaborators to succeed them (CCC 1577). Lightfoot, an Anglican bishop and editor of the letter, held that it "throughout only recognizes two orders, presbyters and deacons," at Corinth. The cards at Philippians 1:1, Acts 20:28 and Titus 1:5-7 set the churches' views side by side.

deep.b: Clement names "overseers and deacons" here (42:4-5), speaks of "the office of overseer" from which blameless men were removed (44:4), and then calls the same men "elders" (44:5; 47:6; 54:2; 57:1). Lightfoot drew the conclusion: "episkopos and presbyteros therefore are synonymes in Clement, as they are in the Apostolic writers," and the letter "throughout only recognizes two orders, presbyters and deacons, as existing at Corinth." The Catholic Catechism uses the same chapters for a different point, that the apostles provided for successors (CCC 861). These are not quite contrary claims: one is about how many offices the letter names, the other about whether the apostles' commission was handed on. Whether a single bishop over the elders is an apostolic order, and when it appeared, is the question of the cards at Philippians 1:1, Acts 20:28, 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1:5-7.

The site's Isaiah, from the Hebrew: "I will make peace your governor and righteousness your taskmaster." The Greek (Swete): "I will give your rulers in peace and your overseers in righteousness." Clement: "I will appoint their overseers in righteousness and their deacons in faith" (42:5). Lightfoot: "Loosely quoted from LXX Is. lx. 17 ... the introduction of the diakonoi is due to misquotation." Clement's argument, that overseers and deacons were "written about many ages before," rests on the Greek, not on the Hebrew, whose verse names no officials at all.

echoes: John 20:21; Matthew 10:40; Acts 1:2-8; Acts 14:23; Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:1-13; Titus 1:5-9; Isaiah 60:17; 1 Corinthians 16:15

title: Aaron's rod
sum: Why be surprised that the apostles appointed leaders, when Moses did the same? Clement retells Numbers 17: the tribes quarreled over the priesthood, Moses sealed twelve rods in the tent of the testimony, and in the morning Aaron's rod had sprouted and borne fruit. Moses knew the outcome, but he staged the test "so that there would be no disorder in Israel."
Clement adds details Numbers does not have: the rods tied and sealed with rings, the keys sealed, the six hundred thousand gathered. They make the point that no one could argue with God's choice.

views.J: Clement treats the story as Scripture written by Moses, whom he calls, with the Greek of Numbers 12:7, "a faithful attendant in the whole house" (43:1), and the prophets as his witnesses. His retelling may draw on Jewish storytelling around the Bible, or on his own art.
views.N: Hebrews 3:5 uses the same verse about Moses, and Hebrews 9:4 places Aaron's rod that budded in the ark.
views.O: The story was chosen because it ends a dispute over who may serve. It can be read as a picture of God choosing ministers, or only as a lesson about God-given order; Clement draws only the second lesson.

echoes: Numbers 16; Numbers 17:1-11; Numbers 12:7; Hebrews 3:2-5; Hebrews 9:4; Exodus 12:37

settings.by: Moses, in Clement's retelling
settings.to: The twelve tribal leaders of Israel in the wilderness
settings.when: When the tribes were quarreling over the priesthood (Numbers 17)
settings.why: To put the choice of the priestly tribe in God's hands, publicly, so that the quarrel would end.
settings.readers: Clement's Corinthian readers, who were to see their own quarrel over church office in Israel's.

title: The apostles' provision, and a wrong at Corinth
sum: The apostles foresaw "that the title of overseer would be fought over." So they appointed leaders and "added a rule" that, if they fell asleep, other tested men should take over. Those appointed this way, with the whole church agreeing, who have served without blame, should not be thrown out. Yet Corinth has done exactly that.

Its key word (44:2) differs in every witness, and its subject ("if they fell asleep") is unnamed; the Catholic Catechism and the Second Vatican Council cite these chapters for succession from the apostles (CCC 861; Lumen Gentium 20). It is also the one place where Clement says plainly what happened at Corinth (44:6).
readings: The apostles made a rule for local churches: when the first overseers died, other approved men would replace them, appointed by respected leaders with the church's consent. The chapter is about the stability of a congregation's elders, and it says nothing of a line of bishops.

The apostles handed on their own work of appointing and overseeing to men who would continue it after them. The chapter is an early witness to the principle that church leaders stand in a line from the apostles, which the Catholic Catechism cites it for (CCC 861).

views.H: For historians the chapter dates the letter: men appointed by the apostles are still alive, so Lake places it "probably not much later than 100." It also shows a church in Rome advising another on its leaders, and shows elders who could be removed by their own congregation.
views.N: The chapter stands beside Acts 14:23, Acts 20:17-35, Titus 1:5 and 2 Timothy 2:2. Like Acts 20:29-30, it says the apostles foresaw strife over leadership.
views.O: The Second Vatican Council and the Catholic Catechism cite the chapter for the apostles' provision for successors (Lumen Gentium 20; CCC 861; 1577). Lightfoot read it as a rule for filling the local office of elder-overseer, "so that vacancies by death should be filled by other approved men." The card on this page asks the question the chapter itself raises: may a congregation remove its ministers?

deep.b:
Three things are uncertain in one sentence. First, the noun: A has epinomē, which Lake takes in the sense "codicil" ("they added a rule"); C has epidomē, "a further gift"; the Latin, legem, "a law"; the Syriac points to "on probation"; the Coptic paraphrases "gave to those who were after them"; and Lightfoot printed a conjecture, epimonē, "permanence" (see the variant). Second, the adverb metaxy, "afterward" or "in the meantime." Third, the subject of "if they fell asleep": the first overseers (Lightfoot), or the apostles (Rothe, as Lightfoot reports him). Lake judges that "the translation is doubtful," and the Plain English Translation keeps the ambiguity of the Greek.

What is not uncertain is the point Clement draws in 44:3: men appointed in this way, who served well, should not be removed. Whatever the provision was, it was meant to keep the church's ministry from being broken off.

The Second Vatican Council says the apostles "took care to appoint successors," passing on their work "as it were, in the form of a testament," and "gave them the order that, when they should have died, other approved men would take up their ministry" (Lumen Gentium 20). The Catechism cites "St. Clement of Rome, Ad Cor. 42, 44" for the apostles' ruling that "on their death other proven men should take over their ministry" (CCC 861), and 42:4 and 44:3 for the apostles choosing collaborators to succeed them (CCC 1577). Lightfoot, an Anglican bishop and an editor of the letter, read the same chapters as showing one office of elder-overseer at Corinth, alongside deacons, and the provision of 44:2 as a rule for filling that office. The questions of succession and of bishops and elders are on the cards at Acts 1:20-26, 2 Timothy 2:2, Philippians 1:1 and Acts 20:28, so they are not repeated here.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a provision for after a death
deep.b: If Lake is right that epinomē here carries the sense "codicil," Clement may be picturing the apostles' work the way one pictures a will. The apostles, like a testator, first named those who would hold their charge (42:4), then added a clause providing for what would happen after those men died (44:2). To remove such men would then be like setting aside the terms of a will, which is how 44:3-4 treats it: "no small sin." This reading is my own, and no source opened here discusses wills in connection with this verse. It builds on Lake's gloss "codicil" and on Rothe's earlier sense "after-enactment," as Lightfoot reports it; Lightfoot rejects both senses of the word as "unwarranted." It overlaps with the Second Vatican Council, which says the apostles passed on their work "in the form of a testament" (Lumen Gentium 20), and with the Catechism's "by will and testament, as it were" (CCC 861). It rests on 42:4 and 44:2-4.

traditions.q: Corinth removed elders who had served "without blame" (44:3-6). May a congregation remove its ordained ministers, and on what grounds? (Whether the apostles have successors is the card at Acts 1:20-26; who chooses a church's ministers is the card at Acts 14:23.) Each row gives what one church's own rules say about removing a parish's pastor.
views: The Code of Canon Law gives the removal of a parish's pastor to the diocesan bishop: "When the ministry of any pastor becomes harmful or at least ineffective for any cause, even through no grave personal negligence, the diocesan bishop can remove him from the parish" (canon 1740). Among the causes it lists are conduct that gravely disturbs church communion, inability to serve, "loss of a good reputation among upright and responsible parishioners or an aversion to the pastor which it appears will not cease in a brief time," grave neglect after a warning, and poor administration (canon 1741). The bishop must first consult two pastors and urge the pastor to resign (canon 1742).

The Statute of the Orthodox Church in America gives the diocesan bishop the power to "appoint, transfer, remove, and grant retirement to Parish Clergy of his Diocese" (article 8), and says the parish priest serves "by virtue of his ordination and canonical appointment" and "cannot vacate his Parish" without the bishop's permission (article 12). Cases of clergy discipline go first to a diocesan church court, and the "deposition of clergy" is among the powers of the Holy Synod (articles 15 and 2).

In the Episcopal Church, a rector may not "be removed there from by the Vestry against the Rector's will," except by the canon's process: if rector or vestry wants the relation dissolved and they cannot agree, either may notify the diocese, the bishop may order mediation, and finally "the Bishop, as final arbiter and judge, shall render a written godly judgment" after consulting the Standing Committee (Canons, Title III, canon 9, section 15).

In the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America's required model constitution, a congregation's call accepted by a pastor is "a continuing mutual relationship and commitment, which shall be terminated only by the pastor's death or, following consultation with the synod bishop, for any of the following reasons," which include "inability to conduct the pastoral office effectively in view of physical disability or mental incapacity." Complaints of ineffective ministry go to the synod bishop, who may investigate with a committee (Model Constitution for Congregations, *C9.05, as amended in 2022).

In the Presbyterian Church in America, a congregation may ask to end its pastor's call: "If any church desires to be relieved of its pastor, a similar procedure shall be observed" as when a minister resigns, with a congregational meeting, but the minister stays until "the Presbytery or its commission" has "dissolved the relation" (Book of Church Order 23-1). Other Reformed bodies have their own rules.

In the United Methodist Church, "Clergy shall be appointed by the bishop, who is empowered to make and fix all appointments," after consultation with the pastor and the committee on pastor-parish relations; but "Consultation is not committee selection or call of a pastor. The role of the committee on pastor-parish relations is advisory" (Book of Discipline, paragraphs 425-426).

The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 describes each church as "an autonomous local congregation of baptized believers" that "operates under the Lordship of Christ through democratic processes" (article 6). The confession itself sets out no procedure for removing a pastor.

echoes: Acts 1:20-26; Acts 14:23; Acts 20:17-35; Titus 1:5-9; 1 Timothy 3:1-7; 1 Timothy 5:17-22; 2 Timothy 2:2; Hebrews 5:1; 1 Peter 5:1-4

title: The righteous were never cast out by the holy
sum: Look into the Scriptures, Clement says, and you will never find the righteous thrown out by holy men. They were hunted, jailed, stoned and killed, but always by the lawless. Daniel was not thrown to the lions by people who feared God, nor the three young men into the furnace by true worshipers. Those who held out "inherited glory and honor."
The argument is sharp: by removing blameless elders, the Corinthians have put themselves on the side of the persecutors in every Bible story.

views.N: The list echoes Hebrews 11:33-38, which joins Daniel's lions and the fire of the furnace, and the stoning of the prophets in Matthew 23:37.
views.J: Clement uses the Greek names of the three young men, Ananias, Azarias and Misael, in the order of their song in the Greek Daniel (part of the Additions to Daniel). He calls the Scriptures true and "given through the Holy Spirit."

echoes: Daniel 3; Daniel 6; Hebrews 11:33-38; Matthew 23:34-37; Acts 7:52; 2 Timothy 3:16

title: Why is there splitting among you?
sum: Cling to the holy, Clement urges, and quotes Psalm 18 in the Greek: with the innocent you will be innocent. Then come his questions: why fights, rage, divisions and war, when there is one God, one Christ, one Spirit and one calling? Why tear apart the members of Christ's body? He reminds them of a saying of the Lord Jesus, woe to the one who turns aside one of the chosen, and of the damage already done: many turned aside, many discouraged, "and your rebellion goes on."

views.N: The chapter gathers Ephesians 4:4-6, Romans 12:5 and 1 Corinthians 12, and a saying of Jesus that joins Matthew 26:24 with Luke 17:2. Whether Clement knew written Gospels or sayings passed on by mouth is argued.
views.J: Both quotations at 46:2-3 are introduced as Scripture. The first matches no known book; the second is a shortened form of the Greek Psalm 18:25-26, which differs in sense from the Hebrew (see the note at 46:3).

echoes: Psalm 18:25-26; Ephesians 4:4-6; Romans 12:4-5; 1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Matthew 26:24; Luke 17:1-2; Matthew 18:6-7; Galatians 5:20

settings.what: A saying of the Lord Jesus
settings.by: Jesus, as Clement quotes him
settings.to: Jesus' disciples, in the Gospels' settings (the Last Supper, Matthew 26:24; a teaching on causing others to stumble, Luke 17:1-2)
settings.when: Clement's form; no Gospel has exactly these words. He joins two sayings
settings.why: To warn that leading God's chosen astray is worse than never being born.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Take up Paul's letter
sum: Clement sends the Corinthians back to "the letter of the blessed Paul the apostle," the letter we call 1 Corinthians. Paul wrote, "truly led by the Spirit," about the parties of Paul, Cephas and Apollos. That old taking of sides was less sinful, because they had followed apostles and an approved man. Now "one or two people" have led "the solid and ancient church of the Corinthians" into rebellion against its elders, and the report has reached outsiders.

views.H: The chapter shows that the Corinthian church still had Paul's letter some decades later and that the Roman church knew it. It is an early use of a letter of Paul by another writer.
views.N: The parties are those of 1 Corinthians 1:12 and 3:4-6. Clement calls Paul and Cephas "apostles" and Apollos a man they had tested (Acts 18:24-28).
views.O: Clement treats Paul's letter as written under the Spirit's guidance but does not call it Scripture; how the New Testament came to be read with the Old is part of the story of the canon.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 1:10-13; 1 Corinthians 3:3-6; Acts 18:24-28; Romans 2:24; 1 Corinthians 7:40; 2 Peter 3:15-16

settings.why: To remind the Corinthians of their own history of factions and of Paul's warning, so that they would see the new revolt as worse, and turn back quickly.

title: The gate of righteousness
sum: "So let us remove this quickly." Clement calls the church to fall before the Master in tears and ask to be brought back to brotherly love. He quotes Psalm 118: "Open the gates of righteousness for me." Of the many gates that stand open, the gate of righteousness is the one in Christ. Gifts of faith, knowledge and wisdom are good, but the greater a man seems, the humbler he should be, seeking what helps everyone.

views.N: The gate is Christ, as in John 10:9. The gifts of 48:5 echo 1 Corinthians 12:8-9, and the rule "what benefits everyone" is Paul's (1 Corinthians 10:24, 33).
views.J: Clement quotes the Greek Psalm 118:19-20, with "Lord" for the divine name (see the note at 48:2).

echoes: Psalm 118:19-20; John 10:7-9; Matthew 7:13-14; 1 Corinthians 12:8-9; 1 Corinthians 8:1; 1 Corinthians 10:24

settings.by: The psalmist (Psalm 118:19-20), quoted by Clement
settings.to: In the psalm, those who keep the gates; the speaker asks to be let in to give thanks
settings.when: Quoted from the Greek Psalms
settings.why: In the psalm, to enter and give thanks; Clement makes the gate of righteousness the way back to love for the divided Corinthians.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). title: What love does
sum: Clement's hymn to love, written to the church that first heard 1 Corinthians 13. Who can explain the bond of God's love? Love joins us to God, "lays a cover over a great number of sins," puts up with everything. It has no split and does not rebel; it "does everything in harmony." In love all God's chosen were made perfect, and in love Christ gave his blood, his flesh for our flesh and his soul for our souls.

views.N: The chapter rewrites 1 Corinthians 13 for a church in rebellion and quotes 1 Peter 4:8 word for word. 49:6 is one of the clearest statements in the letter of Christ's self-giving for us.
views.O: The chapter can be read as a sermon on love and as an early witness to the belief that Christ gave himself in our place (see the note at 49:6 and the topic on the atonement).

echoes: 1 Corinthians 13:1-13; 1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 10:12; Colossians 3:14; John 10:11-15; Galatians 1:4

settings.why: To set before a divided church the love that "has no split" and "does not rebel," and to ask them to pray to be found in it.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Pray to be found in love
sum: Love is beyond explaining, and no one can be found in it unless God counts them worthy. So Clement asks the church to pray for it. All generations since Adam have passed away, but those made perfect in love will be shown openly when Christ's kingdom comes. He joins Isaiah 26:20 and Ezekiel 37:12 into a promise of resurrection, and quotes Psalm 32, as Paul did, on the blessing of forgiveness.

views.N: Clement quotes Psalm 32:1-2 in the same Greek words as Romans 4:7-8, and uses it for forgiveness "through love" where Paul uses it for righteousness by faith.
views.J: Isaiah 26:20 and Ezekiel 37:12 are both quoted in the Greek and joined under one "it is written," two verses with a shared theme read as one promise.

echoes: Isaiah 26:19-20; Ezekiel 37:12-13; Psalm 32:1-2; Romans 4:6-8; 1 Peter 2:12; Luke 19:44

settings.what: A promise to hide and to rise

settings.to: In Isaiah, God's people told to hide until his anger passes; in Ezekiel, the house of Israel, pictured as dry bones
settings.when: Quoted as Scripture
settings.why: To promise that those made perfect in love will be raised when the kingdom comes (50:3).
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Confess, and do not harden your hearts
sum: Clement asks forgiveness for whatever "we" have done through the enemy's attacks, and he asks the leaders of the revolt to look to the hope all share. People who live in fear and love would rather suffer than harm the church's harmony. Better to confess than to harden one's heart, like Korah's band, who "went down alive into Hades," or Pharaoh's army, sunk in the Red Sea.

views.J: Two stories of hardened hearts from the Torah: Korah's revolt against Moses (Numbers 16) and Pharaoh at the sea (Exodus 14). Korah is the closer parallel: a revolt against God-given leaders.
views.N: Jude 11 uses Korah against troublemakers in the church, as Clement does; Hebrews 3:8 warns against hardening hearts.

echoes: Numbers 16:1-35; Psalm 49:14; Exodus 14:23-28; Exodus 15:4; Jude 11; Hebrews 3:7-13

settings.by: The church of God at Rome, writing as one body ("we"); tradition names Clement as the writer
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, addressed as "brothers" and "beloved"
settings.when: Toward the end of the first century (Lake: between 75 and 110, most likely the 90s), after the Corinthians removed some of their elders
settings.why: To move the leaders of the revolt to confess, without excusing them, by joining the Romans with them ("we") and holding up the fate of those who hardened their hearts.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: The sacrifice God wants
sum: God needs nothing from anyone except confession. Clement quotes David three times: "I will confess to the Lord, and it will please him more than a young calf"; "Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise"; and "a broken spirit is the sacrifice for God." The Greek word for confess also means to praise: confession of sin and praise of God are one act.

views.J: All three quotations are from the Greek Psalms (69, 50 and 51), each differing a little from the Hebrew. The theme, that God wants a humble heart more than animals, runs through the Psalms and the prophets (Psalm 50:9-13; Hosea 6:6).
views.N: Hebrews 13:15 uses the same Greek phrase, "a sacrifice of praise," and Acts 17:25 says God needs nothing from human hands.

echoes: Psalm 69:30-32; Psalm 50:9-15; Psalm 51:16-17; Hebrews 13:15; Acts 17:24-25; Hosea 6:6

settings.what: David's words on the sacrifice God wants
settings.by: David, as Clement quotes the Greek Psalms 69:30-32, 50:14-15 and 51:17
settings.to: God, and in Psalm 50 God's people
settings.when: Quoted from the Greek Psalms
settings.why: To show that God wants confession, praise and a broken spirit, not offerings, so that the rebels at Corinth would confess (51:3; 52:1).
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Moses offers himself for the people
sum: Clement reminds the Corinthians of a story they know: Moses on the mountain for forty days, the golden calf below, and God's offer to destroy the people and make Moses a great nation. Moses refuses: "Forgive this people their sin, or blot me out too from the book of the living." "What great love!" Clement cries. The attendant speaks boldly to his Lord and offers to perish with the people.

views.J: The words follow Deuteronomy 9:12-14 and Exodus 32:32 in the Greek. Moses as the one who intercedes for Israel is a theme of the Torah and the Psalms (Psalm 106:23).
views.N: Paul's wish to be cut off for his people (Romans 9:3) is the closest Christian parallel.

echoes: Exodus 32:7-14; Exodus 32:30-32; Deuteronomy 9:9-29; Psalm 106:23; Romans 9:3; Psalm 69:28

settings.what: God and Moses on the mountain
settings.by: God, and then Moses, as Clement quotes Deuteronomy and Exodus
settings.to: Moses on Mount Sinai, and Moses to God
settings.when: While Israel made the golden calf below
settings.why: God tests Moses with an offer to make him a great nation; Moses refuses and asks forgiveness for the people, or to be blotted out with them.
settings.readers: Clement's Corinthian readers, meant to see in Moses a leader who gives himself up for the people's peace (54:1-2).

title: Let the one who caused it leave
sum: Now the practical request. Who among you is noble, tender-hearted, full of love? Let him say: "If the rebellion is because of me, I will step aside. I will go wherever you want, and do what the people tell me. Only let Christ's flock live in peace with the elders who have been appointed." Such a man will win great fame in Christ, and every place will welcome him, because "the earth and all that fills it belong to the Lord."

views.H: The request suggests that the leaders of the revolt were few and known by name, and that leaving Corinth was a real possibility. It is the plainest statement of what Rome hoped would happen.
views.G: Clement himself says that "many left their own cities" to end civil strife (55:1). The language of citizenship in 54:4 belongs to the life of a Greek or Roman city.
views.O: The congregation ("the people") has a voice here: the departing leader will do what it tells him.

echoes: Exodus 32:32; Romans 9:3; Jonah 1:12; Psalm 24:1; 1 Corinthians 10:26; Philippians 1:27; Philippians 3:20

settings.what: The speech Clement asks of the rebels' leader
settings.by: Clement, putting words in the mouth of "whoever among you is noble"
settings.to: The Corinthian church, spoken by one of the leaders of the revolt
settings.when: Toward the end of the first century (Lake: between 75 and 110, most likely the 90s), after the Corinthians removed some of their elders
settings.why: To give the rebels' leaders words they could actually say, a way to end the split with honor.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Those who gave themselves for others
sum: Clement gives examples of self-giving. From the nations: kings who, told by an oracle in time of plague, gave themselves to death for their citizens, and people who left their cities to end civil strife. From the church: Christians at Rome who gave themselves up to chains to ransom others, or sold themselves into slavery to feed others. And from Scripture: Judith, who went out into the enemy camp, and Esther, who risked her life after fasting and humbling herself.

views.H: The report of Christians selling themselves into slavery to feed others is a rare glimpse of the Roman church's charity (see the note at 55:2).
views.J: Clement uses Judith and the Greek Esther, with its prayer in Addition C, as true examples, without introducing them as Scripture. Judith and the Additions to Esther are in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, not in the Hebrew Bible or Protestant Bibles.
views.G: Clement names no pagan king or citizen. Lightfoot gives the kind of story he may mean: Codrus, Bulis and Sperthias, Marcus Curtius, the Decii and Menoeceus, who died for their people, and Lycurgus and Scipio Africanus, who left their cities (see the note at 55:1).

echoes: Judith 8:32-34; Judith 13:15; Esther 4:16; Esther 4:17; John 15:13; 1 Corinthians 9:19; Hebrews 13:3

settings.by: The church of God at Rome, writing as one body ("we"); tradition names Clement as the writer
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, addressed as "brothers" and "beloved"
settings.when: Toward the end of the first century (Lake: between 75 and 110, most likely the 90s), after the Corinthians removed some of their elders
settings.why: To show the leaders of the revolt that leaving for the sake of others is what the best of every people, and the heroes of Scripture, have done.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Accept discipline
sum: Let us pray for those caught in wrong, that they may yield to God's will, and let us accept correction from one another. Clement gathers Scripture on discipline: Psalm 118:18, Proverbs 3:12 in the form of Hebrews 12:6, Psalm 141:5, and the whole promise of Job 5:17-26. God disciplines "as a good Father," so that we may be shown mercy.

views.J: All the quotations are from the Greek. Psalm 141:5 means something different in the Hebrew, and Job 5 is the speech of Eliphaz, quoted as Scripture as Paul also quotes Eliphaz (1 Corinthians 3:19).
views.N: Clement's form of Proverbs 3:12 is word for word that of Hebrews 12:6, and his conclusion follows Hebrews 12:7-11.

echoes: Psalm 118:18; Proverbs 3:11-12; Hebrews 12:5-11; Psalm 141:5; Job 5:17-26; James 5:16; Galatians 6:1

settings.by: The church of God at Rome, writing as one body ("we"); tradition names Clement as the writer
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, addressed as "brothers" and "beloved"
settings.when: Toward the end of the first century (Lake: between 75 and 110, most likely the 90s), after the Corinthians removed some of their elders
settings.why: To ask the whole church to pray for the rebels and to present discipline as a father's love, so that submission would not feel like defeat.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

settings.what: Eliphaz on the blessing of correction
settings.by: Eliphaz the Temanite in Job 5:17-26, quoted by Clement as Scripture ("it says")
settings.to: Job, in his suffering
settings.when: Quoted from the Greek Job
settings.why: In Job, to urge Job to accept God's correction; Clement uses it to show the rebels that discipline from God ends in safety and peace.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Submit to the elders
sum: Clement speaks straight to "you who laid the foundation of the rebellion": submit to the elders, bend the knees of your heart, learn to submit. It is better to be small in Christ's flock than to stand out and be thrown out. Then he quotes Wisdom's warning from Proverbs 1: I called and you did not listen, so I will laugh at your ruin.

From 57:7 to the end of chapter 63, the older of the two Greek manuscripts, Codex Alexandrinus, is missing a leaf. For this stretch the Greek rests on Codex Constantinopolitanus (1056) and the Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions (see the note at 57:7).

views.H: Because of the lost leaf of Codex Alexandrinus, the Greek of 57:7-63:4, the great prayer included, rests on Codex Constantinopolitanus, which Bryennios found in Constantinople in 1875 (Lake's introduction).
views.J: Clement calls Proverbs "the all-excellent Wisdom," a title Eusebius says Hegesippus, Irenaeus "and the whole company of the ancients" used for the book (Church History 4.22.8). He follows the Greek of Proverbs 1:23-33, with "the fear of the Lord" at 1:29.
views.N: "Submit to the elders" is 1 Peter 5:5.

echoes: 1 Peter 5:5; Hebrews 13:17; Prayer of Manasseh 11; Proverbs 1:20-33

settings.by: Wisdom, as Proverbs 1 presents her, quoted by Clement
settings.to: In Proverbs, the simple and the scoffers at the city gates
settings.when: Quoted from the Greek Proverbs
settings.why: Wisdom warns that those who refuse her will call on her too late; Clement aims the warning at the rebels.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Take our advice
sum: Let us obey God's holy name and escape Wisdom's threats. "Accept our advice, and you will have nothing to regret." Clement swears by God, the Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit that whoever keeps God's commands in humility and forbearance will be counted among the saved.

views.N: The oath names God, Christ and the Spirit together, as Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:14 do.
views.O: The verse names God, Christ and the Spirit together in one oath, an early witness that bears on faith in the Trinity; Clement does not explain how the three relate.

echoes: Judges 8:19; Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14; Luke 10:20; Revelation 3:5

title: The great prayer begins
sum: If some disobey "what God has said through us," they put themselves in danger; Rome will be free of that sin. Then the letter becomes a prayer. Clement asks God to keep the number of his chosen unbroken, and turns to address him: "Grant us, Lord, to hope in your name." He praises God in a chain of Old Testament phrases, the one who humbles the proud and lifts the lowly, and prays for those in every need: the afflicted, the fallen, the sick, the hungry, the prisoners.

This prayer (59:2-61:3) is the longest in the letter; Lightfoot traces its echoes in later church prayers, such as the Apostolic Constitutions. The Greek opening of 59:3 has a gap, filled by Lightfoot's "Grant us, Lord."

views.H: The prayer may preserve the language of the Roman church's worship. Lightfoot notes that the Apostolic Constitutions, book 8, is "evidently indebted" to it.
views.J: The praise is woven from the Greek Old Testament (Isaiah 57:15; 1 Samuel 2:6-7; Deuteronomy 32:39; Numbers 16:22), and the petitions match Psalm 146 and the second blessing of the Jewish daily prayer, the Amidah (see the note at 59:4).
views.N: Jesus is God's "beloved servant," as in the prayers of Acts 4:24-30, and the calling "from darkness into light" is that of Acts 26:18 and 1 Peter 2:9.
views.O: The prayer can be read as a window into early Christian worship. Whether the Roman church's words "through us" claim authority over Corinth is discussed in the note at 59:1.

deep.b: The prayer moves the way Jewish prayer moves: praise of who God is (59:3), then petitions (59:4), then confession and a plea for forgiveness (60:1-2), then prayer for peace and for rulers (60:4-61:2), then a closing doxology through a high priest (61:3). Many of its phrases are acts that the second blessing of the Amidah also praises: God holds up the fallen, heals the sick, sets free the bound, puts to death and gives life (Hebrew on Sefaria: somekh noflim ve-rofe cholim u-matir asurim; memit u-mechayeh). The first-century wording of the Amidah is not known, so the shared phrases show a common way of praying, rooted in the Psalms (Psalm 146:7-8; 145:14), rather than a proven borrowing.

echoes: Ephesians 1:18; Isaiah 57:15; 1 Samuel 2:1-10; Luke 1:46-55; Deuteronomy 32:39; Psalm 146:7-9; Acts 4:24-30; Acts 26:18; 1 Peter 2:9; Psalm 100:3

settings.by: The church of God at Rome, praying aloud in the letter
settings.to: God, "Master" and "Lord"; overheard by the Corinthian church, which would hear it read
settings.when: Toward the end of the first century (Lake: between 75 and 110, most likely the 90s), after the Corinthians removed some of their elders
settings.why: To pray for the whole church, the needy and the rulers, and to let the Corinthians hear Rome pray for them, so that their peace becomes a matter of shared prayer.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church hearing the letter read; and Christians since, who have read the prayer as a window into early Roman worship.
views: The prayer's language is echoed in later liturgies, such as the Apostolic Constitutions, book 8.

title: Forgive us
sum: The prayer praises God as the Creator who made the world's order plain to see, faithful, righteous and kind, and asks him to forgive. "Do not count every sin of your slaves." It asks for clean hearts, straight steps, God's face to shine on his people, rescue from those who hate them, and harmony and peace for all who live on the earth, with obedience to God and to "our rulers and governors on the earth."

views.J: The prayer uses God's self-description from Exodus 34:6 ("merciful and compassionate"), the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25, and the "strong hand" and "high arm" of the Exodus.
views.O: The prayer sets obedience to God and to rulers side by side (60:2, 4); the limits of obedience to rulers are set out on the cards at Romans 13:1 and Acts 5:29.

echoes: Exodus 34:6-7; Joel 2:13; Numbers 6:24-26; Psalm 80:3; Deuteronomy 4:34; Romans 13:1-7; 1 Peter 2:13-17

title: For our rulers
sum: God gave the rulers their authority, so the church submits to them in all that does not go against God's will. The prayer asks God to give them health, peace, harmony and steadiness, and to guide them to govern in peace, gentleness and godliness. It ends with praise through Jesus Christ, "the high priest and protector of our souls."
If the letter dates from the 90s, this is a prayer for an emperor in whose reign the church may have suffered (see the note at 61:1).

views.H: The prayer shows a church that sees the Roman state as God-given, even after Nero's persecution (5). Lake is cautious about any persecution under Domitian.
views.N: The prayer carries out 1 Timothy 2:1-2 and stands with Romans 13:1-7 and 1 Peter 2:13-17. God is "King of the ages," as in 1 Timothy 1:17.
views.O: How far obedience to rulers goes is on the cards at Romans 13:1 and Matthew 22:21.

echoes: Romans 13:1-7; 1 Timothy 2:1-2; Titus 3:1; 1 Peter 2:13-17; Daniel 2:21; 1 Timothy 1:17; Hebrews 3:1; 1 Peter 2:25

title: What this letter has said
sum: The prayer over, Clement sums up. The letter has spoken of faith and repentance, real love, self-control, self-restraint and endurance, reminding the Corinthians to please God in a holy way and to live in harmony, "holding no grudges," like the fathers it has held up as examples. Rome writes gladly, knowing it writes to faithful men who have studied "the oracles of God's instruction."

views.G: The letter's key word, harmony (Greek homonoia), was a political word in Greek cities for agreement among citizens, and the summary shows how much of the letter has been an appeal for it.
views.N: The virtue list is close to those of Galatians 5:22-23 and 2 Peter 1:5-7.

echoes: Galatians 5:22-23; 2 Peter 1:5-7; Romans 15:14

settings.by: The church of God at Rome, writing as one body ("we"); tradition names Clement as the writer
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, addressed as "brothers" and "beloved"
settings.when: Toward the end of the first century (Lake: between 75 and 110, most likely the 90s), after the Corinthians removed some of their elders
settings.why: To sum up, to send the messengers and to ask for a quick reply that peace has been made.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Bow the neck and be at peace
sum: It is right to follow such examples, bow the neck, and end the "empty rebellion." The Corinthians will give Rome joy if they obey what it has written "through the Holy Spirit" and cut out their jealousy. Rome has sent faithful men, blameless "from youth to old age," as witnesses between the two churches, because its whole care is that Corinth be at peace soon.

views.H: The messengers who had lived as Christians "from youth to old age" suggest that the Roman church was already decades old, so the letter is well after its founding.
views.O: Readers ask what authority the Roman church claims when it says it wrote "through the Holy Spirit" (see the notes at 59:1 and 63:2, and the card at Matthew 16:18).

echoes: Jeremiah 27:11; Matthew 11:29-30; Acts 15:28; Colossians 4:7-8

title: Blessing
sum: A closing blessing: may the all-seeing God, Master of spirits and Lord of all flesh, who chose Christ and through him "a people that is his own private treasure," give every soul faith, fear, peace, endurance, patience, self-control, purity and self-restraint, through "our high priest and protector Jesus Christ." Codex Alexandrinus resumes here.

views.J: God's titles come from Numbers 16:22 and 27:16, and "a people that is his own private treasure" is the title of Israel in Deuteronomy 14:2.
views.N: Titus 2:14 gives the same title to the church; "high priest" is the title of Hebrews.

echoes: Numbers 16:22; Numbers 27:16; Deuteronomy 14:2; Titus 2:14; 1 Peter 2:9; Hebrews 12:9; Hebrews 13:20-21

settings.by: The church of God at Rome, writing as one body ("we"); tradition names Clement as the writer
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, addressed as "brothers" and "beloved"
settings.when: Toward the end of the first century (Lake: between 75 and 110, most likely the 90s), after the Corinthians removed some of their elders
settings.why: To ask God to give the Corinthians the virtues the letter has urged, so that the letter ends in prayer, not command.
settings.readers: The church at Corinth, after some of its members had removed elders who had served without blame (44:6), led by "one or two people" (47:6). The letter was carried by three Roman messengers to be read aloud there (63:3; 65:1); Dionysius, bishop of Corinth in the time of Soter, bishop of Rome, wrote that his church read a letter from Rome on "the Lord's holy day" and drew advice from the "former" one (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).

title: Send the messengers back
sum: Rome asks Corinth to send back the messengers, Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus, quickly and in peace, with news of the harmony both churches long for. The letter ends with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and a doxology. The title at the end names the sender: "The letter of the Romans to the Corinthians."

views.H: The names Claudius and Valerius may point to men of the imperial household (see the note at 65:1). The closing title names the church, not Clement, as the writer.
views.N: The grace greeting is Paul's (1 Corinthians 16:23; Romans 16:20), and a Fortunatus from Corinth appears in 1 Corinthians 16:17.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 16:17-18; 1 Corinthians 16:23; Romans 16:20; Philippians 4:22
